title: Carmen
facts: Today’s matinee is the Met’s 1,033rd Carmen. The first, on 9 January 1884, drew mixed reviews.
The prelude braids three themes: the bullfighters’ entry, the Toreador refrain, and the motif of Carmen and her fate.
Director Carrie Cracknell (Netflix’s Persuasion) made her Met debut with this staging, at the 2023 New Year’s Eve gala.
^Act\ I:\ Sur\ la\ place,\ chacun\ passe$
Micaëla today: Angel Blue. Met debut in 2017, as Mimì; later a Grammy for the Met’s Porgy and Bess.
Kids’ chorus on the march: conductor Daniele Rustioni sang in La Scala’s boys choir as a child.
Bizet never visited Spain. For Spanish flavor, he went looking for authentic ethnic material.
Hear that brief phrase? The fate motif announces Carmen’s entrance.
Bizet thought the Habanera tune was a folk song. It was by Sebastián Iradier; Bizet credited him in the score.
Under the Habanera: a pedal D held throughout, triplets in the voice, and the flute in its low register.
^Act\ I:\ Carmen!\ Sur\ tes\ pas\ nous\ nous\ pressons\ tous!$
Aigul Akhmetshina, born in Bashkortostan in 1996, also sang Carmen on this staging’s opening night.
^Act\ I:\ Jose!\ Micaela!—Ma\ mere\ je\ la\ vois!$
Piotr Beczała, our Don José, made his Met debut on 19 December 2006, as the Duke in Rigoletto.
The Seguidilla borrows flamenco rhythms and instruments, and drives José to an exasperated high A-sharp shout.
Before Carmen escapes, a disconcerting fragment of the Habanera returns. Bizet revised this finale several times.
This entr’acte is built on the melody José will soon sing offstage, on his way back to Carmen.
Escamillo’s entrance: brass and percussion up front, with the crowd singing along.
^Act\ II:\ Nous\ avons\ en\ tête\ une\ affaire$
Kyle Ketelsen, our Escamillo, joined the Army National Guard planning to fly helicopters. Iowa’s music faculty changed that.
Carmen dances with castanets while a distant cornet calls José to duty, blended into her melody, barely audible.
A muted fate motif on English horn leads in. The Flower Song ends pianissimo, on a sustained high B-flat.
José is swept into the smugglers’ life, and the act closes on a triumphant hymn to freedom.
This entr’acte was first meant for Bizet’s L’Arlésienne. Listen to the woodwinds dialogue and intertwine.
The card trio turns ominous when Carmen joins in: the fate motif underlines her premonition of death.
Micaëla’s aria is framed by horn calls, before and after: listen for them.
As Escamillo leaves, his offstage Toreador refrain sounds confident against José’s growing desperation.
Act IV’s lively entr’acte comes from El criado fingido, a short operetta by Manuel García.
Here come the bullfighters: their march is led by the children’s chorus.
As José kills Carmen, the Toreador refrain rings offstage and the fate motif sounds fortissimo.
